passages.t: Two of Pharaoh's officers in prison
passages.happening:
“Some time later, the king's cupbearer and baker offended their master, the king of Egypt” (verse 1). Pharaoh is angry and puts them in the same prison where Joseph is (verses 2-3). The captain of the guard puts Joseph in charge of them (verse 4).

One night each of them has a dream (verse 5). In the morning Joseph sees that they are upset. He asks, “Why are your faces so downcast today?” (verse 7).

“We both had dreams,” they reply, “but there is no one to interpret them” (verse 8). “Then Joseph said to them, ‘Don't interpretations belong to God? Tell me your dreams’” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The cupbearer served the king his wine. Because he stood close to the king and was trusted with what the king drank, a cupbearer could have real influence. The chief baker ran the making of the royal bread and cakes.

The text does not say what either man did wrong. It says only that they ‘offended’ their master.

In that world dreams were thought to be messages from the gods. Egypt had trained experts to explain them. A papyrus from Egypt now in the British Museum, known as the Chester Beatty dream book and usually dated to the 1200s BC, lists dream after dream with what each was thought to mean, good or bad. That is why the two men are so upset. They believe their dreams matter, and in prison they have no expert to ask.

Notice Joseph. He is a slave, falsely accused, stuck in prison. Yet he notices that two other men look sad, and he asks why. His own trouble has not made him blind to theirs.

And notice his answer. ‘Don't interpretations belong to God?’ Joseph does not claim a skill or a method. He does not have a dream book. He says the meaning belongs to God, and God can give it.
passages.later:
Daniel says almost the same to the king of Babylon: “No wise man, enchanter, medium, or magician can explain to the king the mystery of which he inquires. But there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries” (Daniel 2:27-28).

Nehemiah held the same post as this officer, centuries later, at the court of Persia: “At that time I was the cupbearer to the king” (Nehemiah 1:11).
passages.asks: In his own hard place, Joseph noticed two sad faces and asked why. Ask whether your own troubles have made you stop seeing other people's. Then ask who near you today looks downcast, and whether you could ask them why.

passages.happening:
The cupbearer tells his dream. He saw a vine with three branches. It budded, blossomed and ripened into grapes. “Pharaoh's cup was in my hand, and I took the grapes, squeezed them into his cup, and placed the cup in his hand” (verse 11).

Joseph says, “The three branches are three days” (verse 12). “Within three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore your position” (verse 13).

Then Joseph asks for help. “But when it goes well for you, please remember me and show me kindness by mentioning me to Pharaoh, that he might bring me out of this prison” (verse 14). “For I was kidnapped from the land of the Hebrews, and even here I have done nothing for which they should have put me in this dungeon” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
The dream is easy to love. Everything in it moves fast and goes well: buds, blossoms, ripe grapes, wine in the king's hand. The cupbearer is back at his work.

‘Lift up your head’ was a way of saying ‘restore you to honor’. Think of a man in disgrace, head down, and the king raising his face. Keep the phrase in mind. It will come back with a terrible twist.

Then Joseph speaks of the wrongs done to him, the only time we hear him do so in his years of slavery. He tells the truth plainly. ‘I was kidnapped.’ ‘I have done nothing.’ He does not pretend his suffering is fine. Faith in God, for Joseph, did not mean pretending that injustice was not injustice.

The word he uses for the prison is the same Hebrew word as the ‘pit’ his brothers threw him into (37:24). From one pit to another.

And he asks for help. ‘Remember me.’ He trusts God, and he also asks a man to speak for him. The two go together.
passages.later:
A man dying beside Jesus made the same request: “Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom!” (Luke 23:42). Jesus answered at once, “Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43). Many Christian readers have heard an echo here: Joseph asked to be remembered and was forgotten, while Jesus is the one who remembers.

In the Bible, when God ‘remembers’ someone, he acts for them: “But God remembered Noah” (Genesis 8:1).
passages.asks: Joseph trusted God and still asked for help, and he named the wrong done to him honestly. Ask whether you think faith means never complaining or never asking anyone for help. Then ask whom you could ask today.

passages.happening:
The baker hears the good news and tells his own dream. “There were three baskets of white bread on my head” (verse 16). In the top one were baked goods for Pharaoh, “but the birds were eating them out of the basket on my head” (verse 17).

Joseph says, “The three baskets are three days” (verse 18). “Within three days Pharaoh will lift off your head and hang you on a tree. Then the birds will eat the flesh of your body” (verse 19).

On the third day, Pharaoh's birthday, he holds a feast and “lifted up the heads of the chief cupbearer and the chief baker” (verse 20). He restores the cupbearer and hangs the baker, “just as Joseph had described to them in his interpretation” (verse 22).

“The chief cupbearer, however, did not remember Joseph; he forgot all about him” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The two dreams are built alike: three things, something for the king, the dreamer's own hands or head. But in the baker's dream something is wrong. He does not serve the king. Birds take the king's food from his head.

Joseph tells him the truth. It must have been hard to say. ‘Lift up your head’ now means the opposite: the baker's head will be lifted off. Hanging a body on a tree was a public shame. And for an Egyptian, to have one's body eaten by birds was a special horror. Egyptian religion put great weight on caring for the body after death and burying it properly.

On the third day it all happens as Joseph said. The narrator uses the phrase for both men at once: Pharaoh ‘lifted up the heads’ of both. Then the meanings split apart.

And the last line is the hardest. The cupbearer forgets. The text says it twice: he ‘did not remember’, he ‘forgot all about him’. Joseph had been right, and he had asked for help. And nothing happened. He waits in prison two more full years (41:1).

A word about dreams. This chapter is not a method for reading your own dreams today. Joseph had no system; he said the meaning belonged to God. In the Bible God speaks through dreams at key moments in his plan. Christians differ over whether, and how, he still does. Most agree that anything claimed from a dream must be tested by Scripture, and Israel's law warned against following a ‘dreamer of dreams’ who led people away from God (Deuteronomy 13:1-3).
passages.later:
A psalm cries out the feeling of being forgotten: “How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1). God answers through Isaiah: “Even if she could forget, I will not forget you!” (Isaiah 49:15).

Habakkuk speaks of waiting for what God has said: “Though it lingers, wait for it, since it will surely come and will not delay” (Habakkuk 2:3).
passages.asks: Joseph was forgotten by the one man who could help, and he waited two more years. Ask whether someone has forgotten you when you needed them. Then ask whether you have forgotten someone who is still waiting for you to speak up for them.
